lines.text: A handful of new rows land in a table holding millions. Maintain a stored summary of that table two different ways, and measure both.
Fully rebuilding that summary from scratch barely moves, no matter how small the change was.
Updating it incrementally instead costs a tiny fraction of that — roughly a couple of orders of magnitude less.
Only a handful of rows changed, out of millions sitting in the table.
Does fully rebuilding the dependent summary get any cheaper, just because so little of the underlying data actually moved?
No — rebuilding from scratch reruns the entire defining query regardless of how much actually changed.
Its cost tracks the size of the whole result, never the size of whatever change triggered it.
A full rebuild of a stored result throws away everything it held before and reruns its defining query completely from scratch.
Nothing from the previous version survives the process at all.
The entire result gets recomputed, every single time, whether the underlying data moved by a little or by a lot.
Measure that rebuild twice: once against an untouched table, once right after a handful of new rows get inserted into it.
The two timings, in the end, land within a hair of each other.
A change this small simply doesn't register, because the rebuild was never going to do less work for a smaller change in the first place.
An incrementally maintained version of that same result only ever touches the rows a change actually affects, nothing else.
For a change this small, how much cheaper should maintaining it that way actually be?

tolerated.line: An incrementally maintained version of that same result only ever touches the rows a change actually affects, nothing else.

lines.text: Dramatically cheaper — its cost should track the size of the change itself, not the size of the whole table.
Touching only what a change affects, instead of everything, is exactly the mechanism this topic measures directly next.
Maintain that same summary a second way: update only the one row a new order actually affects, the instant it arrives.
For the identical handful of new rows, that targeted update finishes in a small fraction of the time the full rebuild needed.
Roughly two orders of magnitude cheaper, for keeping exactly the same information current.
An ordinary full rebuild locks out anyone trying to read the stored result while it runs.
Is there any way to update that result without blocking the very queries reading from it?
Yes — a concurrent mode exists specifically so a rebuild and ordinary reads can run side by side.
It trades away nothing about correctness, but it does come with a real requirement, which this topic names next.
Issue an ordinary read against that stored result while an ordinary rebuild is still running underneath it.
That read sits and waits for most of a second, blocked until the rebuild finishes.
Issue the identical read while a concurrent rebuild runs instead, and it comes back in a few thousandths of a second — never blocked at all.

tolerated.line: That read sits and waits for most of a second, blocked until the rebuild finishes.

lines.text: That concurrent mode only works under one condition: the stored result already needs a uniqueness constraint covering every single row.
No partial coverage, and no index built over a computed expression — a plain, row-covering uniqueness guarantee is required.
Without that guarantee in place ahead of time, the concurrent mode simply isn't available at all.
A warehouse engine's own stored summary adds up values from a column that holds approximate, floating-point numbers.
Does that kind of running total still update incrementally, the same way an ordinary total would?
Not reliably — a floating-point running total can force a full rebuild instead.
Floating-point addition doesn't always give the exact same answer regardless of the order values were added in, so an incrementally updated total can quietly drift from a freshly recomputed one.
Adding up values from an approximate, floating-point column can genuinely depend on the order those values arrived in.
That dependency is exactly what forces some engines to fall back to a full rebuild instead of trusting an incremental update.
Switching that column to a fixed-precision numeric type removes the dependency, and keeps the incremental path available.
A cloud warehouse's own stored tables and views don't commit to one strategy ahead of time.
Each one weighs, automatically, whether an incremental update or a full rebuild will actually cost less for its own particular query shape.
Whichever comes out cheaper is the one the engine actually runs.
A warehouse can be told how fresh a stored result needs to stay, as a target it should aim for.
That target is a goal the engine tries to hit, never a strict promise it's bound to keep.
A single slow rebuild can push the real staleness past that target anyway, however carefully it was set.
A full rebuild costs about the same no matter how little actually changed underneath it.
An incremental update instead costs roughly what the change itself costs, nothing more.
A concurrent rebuild trades a strict uniqueness requirement for never blocking an ordinary read, and a freshness target is a goal, never a guarantee.
A stored result is being rebuilt right now, using the concurrent mode this topic just measured. At that exact moment, a dashboard issues an ordinary read against it.
Does that read, though, have to wait for the rebuild to finish first?
No — the concurrent mode exists specifically so a read like that is never blocked.
That's exactly what this topic's own measurement showed directly: the identical kind of read finished in a few thousandths of a second while a concurrent rebuild was still running.
